lesson.subject: anatomy
lesson.title: Airway and root relationships
lesson.summary: A hilum is the entry-exit area on the lung surface; the root is the bundle passing through it.

steps.title: Locate the structures
steps.body: The trachea bifurcates into main bronchi near the transverse thoracic plane, with the carina at the division. Main bronchi divide into lobar and then segmental bronchi, continuing into smaller conducting airways. Terminal bronchioles mark the end of the conducting zone; respiratory bronchioles begin the region in which alveoli participate in gas exchange.

steps.title: Connect structure and function
steps.body: Pulmonary veins tend to lie anterior and inferior in the root, while bronchial relationships differ between right and left. The right superior lobar bronchus arises above the pulmonary artery and is called eparterial. Pulmonary ligaments extend below the roots and accommodate movement. Nerves running in front of or behind the root provide an additional orientation check independent of vessel shape.

steps.title: Why is the right main bronchus a common aspiration route without being an absolute rule?
steps.body: Its typical wider caliber, shorter length and more vertical alignment make entry mechanically more likely for many aspirated objects. However, body position, object size, airflow and distal branching influence where material finally lodges. An upright route and a supine route may favor different downstream segments. The anatomy supports a tendency rather than certainty. A complete answer states the usual right-sided geometry and then explains why clinical distribution cannot be inferred from that feature alone.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: A hilum is the entry-exit area on the lung surface; the root is the bundle passing through it. Bronchi, pulmonary vessels, bronchial vessels, lymphatics and autonomic fibers share that gateway. At the right root the pulmonary artery is anterior to the bronchus; on the left it is superior, summarized as RALS. The right main bronchus is typically wider, shorter and more vertical, but an aspirated object's final site also depends on posture and branching.
